newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Tokyo, HK shares soar on Dow, Philippines battered.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo, HK shares soar on Dow, Philippines battered.

text.p: Tokyo and Hong Kong stock markets ended sharply higher on Wednesday, propelled by Wall Street's rally overnight, but the gains were limited in other markets due to generally negative sentiment.
Philippine stocks were hammered by fears of a shakeout in the property sector and expectations of poor corporate earnings.
U.S. economic data released on Tuesday turned out more favourable than the market had anticipated and sent stocks and bonds soaring.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 179 points, or 2.65 percent, to 6,962 points -- marking the second-largest point rise in a single day.
The closely watched Employment Cost Index - a key measure of wage costs - rose a less-than-expected 0.6 percent in the first quarter, while new orders for large durable goods items fell 3.0 percent.
The news on inflation calmed fears the Federal Reserve would need to tighten interest rates soon.
When Tokyo trading resumed after Tuesday's national holiday, stocks soared nearly 500 points, the key 225-share Nikkei average ending at its highest level since December 30, 1996.
At the close, the average was up 480.75 points, or 2.57 percent, to 19,151.12.
"The surge has erased one unclear factor that Tokyo has worried about," Seiki Orimi, manager of stock information services at Dai-Ichi Securities Co Ltd, said of the outlook for the U.S. market.
Similarly, Hong Kong stocks posted their biggest point gain in more than two months, with the blue chip Hang Seng Index jumping 302.88 points, or 2.40 percent, to close at 12,903.30.
"The pressure to raise interest rates is smaller now and we believe the possibility for a rise in May is not that large," said Stanley Ng, research manager at Mansion House Research.
The positive sentiment failed to carry over into the Philippines, which again fell victim to heavy selling.

Fear of weak corporate earnings and talk its bank and property markets may experience problems similar to those recently seen in Thailand led the Manila share index down 60.27 points, or 2.23 percent, to end at 2,648.17 points.
It had shed more than five percent on Tuesday.
"Sentiment is very weak due to companies' profits that were below expectations," said Lawrence de Leon, analyst at Dharmala Securities Phils.
The Central Bank moved to calm investors' fears, saying it did not expect them to withdraw funds after the stock market slump.
It also raised the interest rate it charges on overnight loans to 11 percent from 10.25 percent.
Some market participants said the selloff was overdone.
"I don't see any fundamental economic reason for this...I think the market has over-reacted," said Roman Azanza, director of Crosby UBP Securities.
Stocks in Taiwan also turned lower due to profit-taking, shedding 106.78 points, or 1.24 percent, to close at 8,485.66.
Elsewhere, the U.S. rally pushed other indices into the plus side, although the gains were capped by investor unease.
"When the Dow is up it provides a slight cushion, and reduces the selling a bit," said Ami Moris, a vice president at Capitalcorp in Kuala Lumpur.
But, she added, "we're still in a downward trend. I think it's premature to say we've seen the worst."
Australia's All Ordinaries Index gave up some early gains to end 8.9 points, or 0.36 percent, higher at 2,488.0, after touching a record high 2,515.1 shortly after the opening.
Thai stocks rebounded from Tuesday's selloff and closed 2.70 points, or 0.41 percent, higher at 661.29 points, while those in Jakarta were up 4.819 points, or 0.74 percent, to 652.049.
Malaysian shares were up 20.66 points, or 1.95 percent, to 1,080.17, bolstered by news the government would allow Tenaga Nasional to raise its electricity rates.
Singapore's Straits Times Index gained 14.06 points, or 0.71 percent, to close at 2,004.26 points.
South Korean shares were off 0.82 of a point at 703.23 in listless trading. Ssangyong Group shares were mixed after news it would restructure its business.
